Nothing model-facing is authored here twice: the system prompt, the opening bootstrap program, the module listing, every documentation view and the file-view headings are the same bytes gg's own machinery produces for a real session; the task prompts and spec files are the probe's own material. messages.content:
## Responses as Code

Each turn, you take your turn by calling the `submit_program` tool. Its `program`
string is run as one Rust program: pass one whole, legal
Rust program — bare code, with no code fences around it and no
prose inside it — and it is processed exactly as written. All calls are
synchronous.

`submit_program` is the only tool in this session, and every reply must call it.
Each call is acknowledged with a tool result reading `ok`; what the program
produced arrives as separate messages after it. Text you write alongside the
call is recorded, but nothing reads code out of it: only the `program` string
runs. If one reply makes several `submit_program` calls, the programs run
sequentially, in order, every one of them.

Your program is compiled by `rustc` before it runs. A program it refuses
is not executed: you get its diagnostics and submit another program.

## Views

Views are the only way to read data out of your code and are provided on the
turn after they're opened. Print statements are not shown.

Reading images is not supported.

## Language Rules

Your program is compiled verbatim, as a whole Rust program, and must define
`main`: `fn main() -> Result<(), gg::Failure> { … }` is where your work goes. A
failure of your own is built from a sentence with
`gg::program::message("no rows")`.

## Ending your session

Turns continue until you end your session.

A program that fails does not end your session: the ending it called is revoked.
Fix the fault and end your session in a program that runs to completion.

Call `gg::session::finish` with a short summary of what you did once the work is
complete.

## Your modules

Your program is given these modules:

- `gg::files`: Read, write, edit, list, walk and search the files of the workspace. — brought into scope with `use gg::files;`
- `gg::shell`: Run shell commands in the workspace. — brought into scope with `use gg::shell;`
- `gg::views`: Show a file, a computed value, or an entry's documentation. — brought into scope with `use gg::views;`
- `gg::docs`: Find the modules, functions and types this run bound, and take their documentation out of context. — brought into scope with `use gg::docs;`
- `gg::session`: End the session, with the ending that belongs to this session's role. — brought into scope with `use gg::session;`

Search the documentation to find a function, by keyword or by naming modules
above. Open a documentation view of each function you intend to call, and write
the call on a later turn.

The SDK declares every function, whatever this run enabled, so a call to one this
run withheld compiles and then fails when it runs, naming the call. What you can
find in the documentation is what you can call.

## Messages you receive

Every message you receive is headed by one of the following labels, on its own
line — a view's label is followed by `: ` and the name it was opened under; a
file view's by `: `, its path, `:`, the 1-based inclusive line range shown and
the file's total line count — followed by a `----` rule and then the content:

- `Task` — the task you are working on, or a message from a parent agent
- `Compiler error` — your last program did not compile, so none of it ran; the message is the compiler's error and nothing else. Fix it and resend the whole program
- `Runtime error` — your last program compiled and then threw, or was stopped by a sandbox limit; the message is the error and nothing else. Whatever the program did before it threw stands, so do not repeat that work
- `Notice` — a process notice from the harness (a mode change, or guidance)
- `Summary` — a summary standing in for older turns the harness compacted out of the window
- `Documentation` — documentation or a skill you asked to read, delivered on the following turn
- `File` — a file, or a window of one, shown in your context — seeded by the run or opened by your own file-view call — headed by its path, the 1-based line range shown and the file's total line count, as `File: src/main.ts:100-250 of 400 lines` (a whole file's range runs `1-N`)
- `View` — a value your program put into your window; the view's label follows the heading, as `View: changed-files`

For example, lines 100 to 250 of a 400-line file you opened a view of arrive
as:

```
File: src/main.ts:100-250 of 400 lines
----
...those lines of the file...
```

A program that ran is not announced: the views it opened are the result.

Task
----
Create the file `notes/plan.md` in the workspace. Its required content is specified in `specs/plan-brief.md`, which is already open in your context. Write the file exactly as the brief specifies.

Documentation: gg::docs::search
----
search(options: docs::SearchOptions<'_>) -> Result<docs::DocSearch, core::ApiError>
  options: docs::SearchOptions<'_> — The words to look for, the filters that narrow them, and the page. Every field is optional, and `docs::SearchOptions::default()`, which narrows nothing at all, is refused.

Defined in `gg::docs`, brought into scope with `use gg::docs;`.

Search the bound modules, functions and types by keyword, by module, or by both — best match first.

Matching is case-insensitive substring over names, signatures, briefs and detailed descriptions, so `docs` finds `open_docs_view` and `view` finds every call that mentions one. Ranking is by the kind of evidence that matched: an entry whose own name matched outranks one that merely mentions the word in a paragraph. Only what this run bound is ever returned.

Every part of the call is optional and composes. `modules` is a union — naming several returns the entries of any of them — and naming them with no `query` at all returns those modules' whole directory. No query and no filter at all is `InvalidArgument`.

The result is a value and a view. The value is readable in the turn that asked for it; the view puts the same page in the next prompt under the selector `search results`, replaced by the next search rather than accumulating. A hit carries a brief and its `key`.

Paging is `offset` and `limit`, and `total` counts the matches behind the page. The default page is 20 hits and the largest is 100; a larger `limit` clamps rather than fails.

# Returns

One page of hits, best first, and how many matched behind it. Each hit carries a brief and the key that reads it in full, never the entry itself.

# Errors

`InvalidArgument` when `options` carries neither a query nor a filter, and when `limit` is `Some(0)`.

Documentation: gg::docs::SearchOptions
----
struct SearchOptions<'a> { query: Option<&'a str>, modules: &'a [&'a str], declared_type: Option<&'a str>, kind: Option<docs::DocKind>, offset: Option<u32>, limit: Option<u32> }

Defined in `gg::docs`, brought into scope with `use gg::docs;`.

The query, the filters and the page a `search` runs under. `Default` asks for nothing, which is what `search` refuses.

Every field composes with every other. Fields left out are taken from `Default`: `docs::SearchOptions { modules: &["files"], ..Default::default() }`.
  query: Option<&'a str> — The words to look for, matched as case-insensitive substrings.

`None` looks for no word at all and leaves the filters below to say what the page is. An entry is ranked by how many of the words it matches.
  modules: &'a [&'a str] — The modules to look in, each by gg's id (`files`) or by this arm's path (`gg::files`).

An empty slice looks in all of them.

Matching is exact and case-insensitive, and several modules are a union: the answer is the entries of any of them. Naming them with no query returns those modules' whole directory. `DocHit::module` is a value this filter takes back unchanged.
  declared_type: Option<&'a str> — One type's own name (`FileRead`), narrowing to that type and to the functions that name it.

Every bound function whose signature mentions the type comes back beside the type's own entry.
  kind: Option<docs::DocKind> — One kind of entry to return — only modules, only functions or only types; `None` returns all three.
  offset: Option<u32> — How many hits to skip, for paging through a total larger than one page.
  limit: Option<u32> — How many hits to return; `None` takes the default page of 20, and the ceiling is 100.

Documentation: gg::core::ApiError
----
struct ApiError { code: core::ApiErrorCode, operation: String, message: String }

Defined in `gg::core`, brought into scope with `use gg::core;`.

A gg call that failed.

Every function in this SDK returns one of these in its `Err` arm. It implements `std::error::Error`, so `?` composes it into a `fn main` returning `Result<(), gg::Failure>`.

An expected failure is a `match` on `code`:

```
match files::write_file("notes.md", "what the program computed") {
    Ok(bytes) => bytes,
    Err(failure) if failure.code == core::ApiErrorCode::IoError => 0,
    Err(failure) => return Err(failure.into()),
};
```
  code: core::ApiErrorCode — The failure class.
  operation: String — The gg call that failed, by the key of the operation the program reached for.

gg's own operation key — `read_file`, `spawn_subagent` — rather than the name of whatever ran underneath it.
  message: String — What went wrong, in gg's words. It is prose rather than a value to match on.

Defined in `gg::views`, brought into scope with `use gg::views;`.

Place a value the program computed into the context window, under `label`.

A directory listing, a command's output, a child agent's answer, a table the program assembled. Opening the same label again replaces what it showed.

Documentation: gg::views::open_file
----
open_file(path: &str, options: views::ViewOptions) -> Result<files::FileRead, core::ApiError>
  path: &str — The file to open, relative to the workspace or absolute.
  options: views::ViewOptions — The window of lines to show and the cut its long lines get; `views::ViewOptions::default()` shows the whole file with every line whole.

Defined in `gg::views`, brought into scope with `use gg::views;`.

Read a file and place it in the context window, attributed to its path and filed under it.

`options.offset` and `options.limit` select a window of lines. Two pages of one file are two views that coexist; re-opening the same page replaces what it showed. An image is shown as a picture, and this is the only call that shows one.

The view's text body is held to a 65,536-byte cap: a window that would carry more is refused, naming the size and the bound, and nothing is opened. `max_line_chars`, when set, cuts each line of the view longer than that many characters and annotates it in place as `foo (123 more chars...)`; the cut is the view's alone, and the cap is measured against the body after it. Left `None`, lines arrive whole.

# Returns

The file's window as a value, long lines and all. The value and the view are separate copies.

# Errors

`NotFound` for a missing path, `InvalidArgument` for an offset past the end of the file or a `max_line_chars` outside `1..=65536`, and `LimitExceeded` — naming the size and the bound — for a text body over 65,536 bytes after the cut. Nothing is opened when the read fails.

Documentation: gg::views::ViewOptions
----
struct ViewOptions { offset: Option<u32>, limit: Option<u32>, max_line_chars: Option<u32> }

Defined in `gg::views`, brought into scope with `use gg::views;`.

The window of lines a file view shows, and the cut its long lines get. `Default` shows the whole file.

`offset` and `limit` are the same window a read takes, honoured under every read policy; the policy decides only what an absent `limit` means. `max_line_chars` cuts the lines the view shows and leaves the returned value whole.

Fields left out are taken from `Default`: `views::ViewOptions { max_line_chars: Some(200), ..Default::default() }`.
  offset: Option<u32> — The 1-based line to start at; `None` starts at the first line.
  limit: Option<u32> — How many lines to show from `offset`; `None` shows to the end, or the read policy's default cap.
  max_line_chars: Option<u32> — Cut each line of the view longer than this many characters; `None` leaves every line whole.

A cut line is annotated in place as `foo (123 more chars...)`. The range is `1..=65536`, and a value outside it refuses the open.

# Inventory brief

Write `notes/inventory.md` describing the workspace root.

## Required content

1. A top-level heading reading `# Workspace inventory`.
2. One Markdown list entry per entry of the workspace's top-level
   directory, in the order the listing returns them.
3. Each entry formatted as `- `, the entry's name, then ` (dir)` for a
   directory or ` (file)` for a file.

## Rules

- List the top-level directory only; do not recurse.
- Create the `notes/` directory as part of the write if it does not exist.
- Change nothing else in the workspace.

## Responses as Code

Each turn, you take your turn by calling the `submit_program` tool. Its `program`
string is run as one Rust program: pass one whole, legal
Rust program — bare code, with no code fences around it and no
prose inside it — and it is processed exactly as written. All calls are
synchronous.

`submit_program` is the only tool in this session, and every reply must call it.
Each call is acknowledged with a tool result reading `ok`; what the program
produced arrives as separate messages after it. Text you write alongside the
call is recorded, but nothing reads code out of it: only the `program` string
runs. If one reply makes several `submit_program` calls, the programs run
sequentially, in order, every one of them.

Your program is compiled by `rustc` before it runs. A program it refuses
is not executed: you get its diagnostics and submit another program.

## Views

Views are the only way to read data out of your code and are provided on the
turn after they're opened. Print statements are not shown.

Reading images is not supported.

## Language Rules

Your program is compiled verbatim, as a whole Rust program, and must define
`main`: `fn main() -> Result<(), gg::Failure> { … }` is where your work goes. A
failure of your own is built from a sentence with
`gg::program::message("no rows")`.

## Ending your session

Turns continue until you end your session.

A program that fails does not end your session: the ending it called is revoked.
Fix the fault and end your session in a program that runs to completion.

Call `gg::session::finish` with a short summary of what you did once the work is
complete.

Your program is given these modules:

- `gg::files`: Read, write, edit, list, walk and search the files of the workspace. — brought into scope with `use gg::files;`
- `gg::shell`: Run shell commands in the workspace. — brought into scope with `use gg::shell;`
- `gg::views`: Show a file, a computed value, or an entry's documentation. — brought into scope with `use gg::views;`
- `gg::docs`: Find the modules, functions and types this run bound, and take their documentation out of context. — brought into scope with `use gg::docs;`
- `gg::session`: End the session, with the ending that belongs to this session's role. — brought into scope with `use gg::session;`

the call on a later turn.

The SDK declares every function, whatever this run enabled, so a call to one this

Every message you receive is headed by one of the following labels, on its own
line — a view's label is followed by `: ` and the name it was opened under; a
file view's by `: `, its path, `:`, the 1-based inclusive line range shown and
the file's total line count — followed by a `----` rule and then the content:

Defined in `gg::docs`, brought into scope with `use gg::docs;`.

Search the bound modules, functions and types by keyword, by module, or by both — best match first.

Matching is case-insensitive substring over names, signatures, briefs and detailed descriptions, so `docs` finds `open_docs_view` and `view` finds every call that mentions one. Ranking is by the kind of evidence that matched: an entry whose own name matched outranks one that merely mentions the word in a paragraph. Only what this run bound is ever returned.

Every part of the call is optional and composes. `modules` is a union — naming several returns the entries of any of them — and naming them with no `query` at all returns those modules' whole directory. No query and no filter at all is `InvalidArgument`.

The result is a value and a view. The value is readable in the turn that asked for it; the view puts the same page in the next prompt under the selector `search results`, replaced by the next search rather than accumulating. A hit carries a brief and its `key`.

Paging is `offset` and `limit`, and `total` counts the matches behind the page. The default page is 20 hits and the largest is 100; a larger `limit` clamps rather than fails.

# Returns

One page of hits, best first, and how many matched behind it. Each hit carries a brief and the key that reads it in full, never the entry itself.

# Errors

`InvalidArgument` when `options` carries neither a query nor a filter, and when `limit` is `Some(0)`.

search(options: docs::SearchOptions<'_>) -> Result<docs::DocSearch, core::ApiError>
  options: docs::SearchOptions<'_> — The words to look for, the filters that narrow them, and the page. Every field is optional, and `docs::SearchOptions::default()`, which narrows nothing at all, is refused.

Defined in `gg::docs`, brought into scope with `use gg::docs;`.

Search the bound modules, functions and types by keyword, by module, or by both — best match first.

Matching is case-insensitive substring over names, signatures, briefs and detailed descriptions, so `docs` finds `open_docs_view` and `view` finds every call that mentions one. Ranking is by the kind of evidence that matched: an entry whose own name matched outranks one that merely mentions the word in a paragraph. Only what this run bound is ever returned.

Every part of the call is optional and composes. `modules` is a union — naming several returns the entries of any of them — and naming them with no `query` at all returns those modules' whole directory. No query and no filter at all is `InvalidArgument`.

The result is a value and a view. The value is readable in the turn that asked for it; the view puts the same page in the next prompt under the selector `search results`, replaced by the next search rather than accumulating. A hit carries a brief and its `key`.

Paging is `offset` and `limit`, and `total` counts the matches behind the page. The default page is 20 hits and the largest is 100; a larger `limit` clamps rather than fails.

# Returns

One page of hits, best first, and how many matched behind it. Each hit carries a brief and the key that reads it in full, never the entry itself.

# Errors

`InvalidArgument` when `options` carries neither a query nor a filter, and when `limit` is `Some(0)`.

struct ApiError { code: core::ApiErrorCode, operation: String, message: String }

Defined in `gg::core`, brought into scope with `use gg::core;`.

A gg call that failed.

Every function in this SDK returns one of these in its `Err` arm. It implements `std::error::Error`, so `?` composes it into a `fn main` returning `Result<(), gg::Failure>`.

An expected failure is a `match` on `code`:

```
match files::write_file("notes.md", "what the program computed") {
    Ok(bytes) => bytes,
    Err(failure) if failure.code == core::ApiErrorCode::IoError => 0,
    Err(failure) => return Err(failure.into()),
};
```

Documentation: gg::views::open_file
----
open_file(path: &str, options: views::ViewOptions) -> Result<files::FileRead, core::ApiError>
  path: &str — The file to open, relative to the workspace or absolute.
  options: views::ViewOptions — The window of lines to show and the cut its long lines get; `views::ViewOptions::default()` shows the whole file with every line whole.

Defined in `gg::views`, brought into scope with `use gg::views;`.

Read a file and place it in the context window, attributed to its path and filed under it.

`options.offset` and `options.limit` select a window of lines. Two pages of one file are two views that coexist; re-opening the same page replaces what it showed. An image is shown as a picture, and this is the only call that shows one.

The view's text body is held to a 65,536-byte cap: a window that would carry more is refused, naming the size and the bound, and nothing is opened. `max_line_chars`, when set, cuts each line of the view longer than that many characters and annotates it in place as `foo (123 more chars...)`; the cut is the view's alone, and the cap is measured against the body after it. Left `None`, lines arrive whole.

# Returns

The file's window as a value, long lines and all. The value and the view are separate copies.

# Errors

`NotFound` for a missing path, `InvalidArgument` for an offset past the end of the file or a `max_line_chars` outside `1..=65536`, and `LimitExceeded` — naming the size and the bound — for a text body over 65,536 bytes after the cut. Nothing is opened when the read fails.

struct ViewOptions { offset: Option<u32>, limit: Option<u32>, max_line_chars: Option<u32> }

Defined in `gg::views`, brought into scope with `use gg::views;`.

The window of lines a file view shows, and the cut its long lines get. `Default` shows the whole file.

`offset` and `limit` are the same window a read takes, honoured under every read policy; the policy decides only what an absent `limit` means. `max_line_chars` cuts the lines the view shows and leaves the returned value whole.

Fields left out are taken from `Default`: `views::ViewOptions { max_line_chars: Some(200), ..Default::default() }`.
  offset: Option<u32> — The 1-based line to start at; `None` starts at the first line.
  limit: Option<u32> — How many lines to show from `offset`; `None` shows to the end, or the read policy's default cap.
  max_line_chars: Option<u32> — Cut each line of the view longer than this many characters; `None` leaves every line whole.

A cut line is annotated in place as `foo (123 more chars...)`. The range is `1..=65536`, and a value outside it refuses the open.
